transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-04-10 | Start: 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE); Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE); Sarah Nguyen (AstraHead ML); Carlos Mendes (Astra infra); Olivia Park (CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — audio ok for folks?
[00:06] Sarah: Yeah, good here.
[00:09] Maya: Cool. Agenda — quick recap of last week, then Liam will walk through the benchmark comparisons we ran vs the baseline provider, show latency and throughput numbers, then open for questions and plan next tests.
[00:20] Carlos: Sounds good.

-- Summary / Key numbers up-front --
[00:30] Liam: Alright, jumping in. We re-ran the benchmark harness against your sample workload and the baseline provider image you gave us. High level numbers: p50 latency on Redwood hosted API for your 512-token average requests is ~28ms per request (that's per chunk), p95 is ~140ms. Baseline provider p95 is ~220ms in the same config. For throughput, on a single reserved instance equivalency Redwood sustained ~1,700 tokens/sec vs baseline ~1,200 tokens/sec. Cost-ish ballpark for your workload: Redwood is coming in ~20% lower per token in these runs when using our recommended batching + int8 quantization profile.
[01:10] Olivia: Wait, those p95 numbers — are they end-to-end on your hosted stack or single-node inference?
[01:17] Liam: Good question. These are end-to-end across Redwood's hosted inference path in the test region we used — includes networking to the instance, marshalling, and runtime. We annotated the results with microbenchmarks so you can see runtime-only vs end-to-end. Runtime-only p95 is closer to 110ms, so networking+overhead adds about 30ms in that environment.
[01:35] Sarah: And is the baseline you're comparing to the vendor-managed endpoint from your spreadsheet — the one labelled 'Baseline-CloudX'?
[01:41] Maya: Yes, 'CloudX' is the label we used for the customer's baseline provider. The baseline tests were run with their default runtime and the same model weights — we tried to keep tokenization and prompts identical.
[01:52] Carlos: There might be some difference in sequence padding and batching config — did you normalize those?
[01:56] Liam: We did. We harmonized batch sizes and used the same token distribution. There are minor differences in kernel selection but we captured that. We also attached the raw logs.

[02:10] Speaker 1 (maybe Liam): Okay so digging into the p95 tail — Redwood's tail improved when we enabled continuous KV cache for prefix-heavy requests. With KV cache on, p50 dropped to 18ms and p95 to ~95ms for the cached routes. Baseline provider doesn't have an equivalent persistent KV cache configured in the tests, so that delta is part of what you're seeing.
[02:40] Sarah: That's interesting — so KV cash? sorry, KV cache — how transparent is that to our app? Is it API-level caching or something inside the runtime?
[02:48] Liam: It's inside the runtime with an opt-in prefix cache. From the app side you can mark routings or conversational threads to be cached. We expose controls via the API, but it doesn't require you to change tokenization or model code. We call out consistency and eviction policies in the docs.
[03:05] Olivia: Are there any security/residency implications — where is the KV cache stored, is it customer-isolated?
[03:12] Maya: For hosted POC we use tenant-isolated caches in our cluster — data is not mixed; in Dedicated or Private deployments you get full customer control and you can pin cache stores to VPC. SE can follow up with exact encryption and KMS details.

[03:30] Liam: Next — quantization. We tested int8 and a mixed int8/4 profile. Int8 gave us a ~1.6x throughput lift with modest quality delta on your eval set — we measured a 2.3% degradation on rouge-like metrics for the generative tasks but for your classification/rerank routes degradation was <1%. The baseline provider didn't enable the same quantization profile.
[03:55] Carlos: How does quantization affect cost? Is the 20% lower number you quoted mostly driven by quantization or by batching/throughput?
[04:02] Liam: It's a combination. Batching and smarter kernel choice deliver base cost improvement, quantization compounds it. Rough split: ~10-12% from batch/serving efficiency + ~6-8% from int8 in our runs.

[04:20] Sarah: We care a lot about regressing on the NPS/regression metric — that 2.3% on rouge for generative is a red flag. Could we do a hybrid where critical routes are fp16 and bulk routes int8?
[04:29] Liam: Yes, route-level quantization is supported. You can pin model variants per route. That's actually what we recommend for production: keep sensitive routes on higher precision, bulk inference on quantized variants.

[04:40] Olivia: Did you run 99th percentile numbers? The p95 is good but our production incidents are driven by 99th.
[04:46] Liam: We're collecting 99th now — initial 99th for Redwood hosted was ~320ms without KV cache, and with KV cache it dropped to ~180ms for cached routes. Baseline 99th was around ~480ms in their test. But we agreed we need to run more stable 99th tests under longer sustained load — that's one of the follow-ups.

[05:10] Maya: Quick note: test harness specifics and raw CSVs are attached in the sheet I'll share after the call. There might be some timestamp mis-alignments in the first batch — we flagged those rows.

[05:24] Carlos: On the throughput numbers, is that measured as tokens/sec aggregated across concurrent connections or per instance?
[05:30] Liam: Tokens/sec per instance-equivalent under the same concurrency pattern you provided. We scaled concurrency to match your production approximate QPS.

[05:45] Sarah: Is there any variance by model size — we run a 7B and a 70B-ish variant for heavier summarization — these tests were on which model?
[05:52] Liam: These runs were on the 13B variant you shipped to us for the pilot. We did a quick 7B run and 70B simulation — 7B was predictably faster (roughly 2.2x tokens/sec vs 13B) and the 70B needs a different instance class and had worse tail latency. If you want we'll run a dedicated 70B bench next.

[06:15] Olivia: For the 70B we probably would want Dedicated — is the Dedicated latency advantage only about tail or across-the-board?
[06:22] Liam: Dedicated helps across the board — predictable throughput, less noisy neighbors, and you can pick GPU type. Tail improves significantly because you avoid multitenant scheduling jitter. For some of our customers tail p99 dropped 30-40% when switching to Dedicated with pinned instances.

[06:40] Speaker 2 (Sarah, or mis-labeled): There's a lot of tradeoffs — we need to quantify business impact. For example, if p95 reduces from 220ms to 140ms we need to map that to user-facing latency and conversion uplift.
[06:52] Maya: Agreed. We can help model the ROI. We'll include a cost/lift model alongside the raw benchmarks.

[07:00] Carlos: A couple of infra questions — network egress between region to region, and VPC peering for Private. Does Redwood's hosted option keep data in region?
[07:08] Liam: Yes, region locality is enforced — you can pin region per route. For Private or Dedicated you get VPC endpoints and peering. For POC hosted we used the test us-west region.

[07:20] Sarah: About compliance: we need SOC2 type II and data at rest encryption for this POC to proceed beyond internal validation.
[07:27] Maya: We have the SOC2 documentation and a summary of our KMS key handling; I'll share the security pack. For Dedicated/Private we support customer-managed KMS.

[07:40] Olivia: One thing I noticed in the logs you sent — there were some spikes at minute 18 in run 3. Any idea?
[07:46] Liam: We saw a spike where the runtime did a kernel swap because of a longer-than-usual sequence hitting the batching window. We have heuristics now to avoid swapping mid-request, but we want to reproduce with your exact trace to confirm. That is on the follow-up list.

[08:05] Sarah: Can we talk briefly about batching param choices? Our production tends to use smaller, latency-sensitive requests. If we increase batch size to optimize cost, how badly does p95 degrade?
[08:17] Liam: There's a curve. In our tests, increasing max batch from 8 to 32 increased tokens/sec by ~40% but p95 for latency-sensitive short requests rose by ~60ms on average. That's why we recommend dynamic batching plus route-level batch caps so critical routes stay low-latency.

[08:40] Carlos: Any changes required on our SDK? We want minimal changes to adopt caching and quantized variants.
[08:46] Liam: Minimal. We have flags in the API for variant selection and cache hints. SDK changes are small — a helper to mark a conversation id as cacheable and to choose model_variant param.

[09:00] Olivia: What's the fallback behavior if a quantized variant regresses in quality?
[09:04] Liam: We support automatic fallback to a pinned high-precision variant on quality regression signal. You can set thresholds and we can route traffic back. We also support canary rollouts.

[09:18] Maya: Ok I want to call out the specific delta numbers again so we have them on record: p95: Redwood 140ms vs Baseline 220ms. p99: Redwood ~320ms (no KV)/180ms (with KV) vs Baseline ~480ms. Throughput per instance: Redwood ~1,700 tokens/sec vs Baseline ~1,200 tokens/sec. Cost delta ~20% lower with our recommended configs.

[09:50] Sarah: Those are promising. We need to validate on the 70B route and also run a longer 6-hour sustained run to see noise and outliers.

[09:59] Liam: Agreed — we'll schedule the sustained run. Also we'll run a 99th/99.9th percentile collection as part of that.

[10:10] Carlos: For the sustained run, we will provide a replay of prod traces — format is the same as what we sent?
[10:15] Sarah: Yes, we'll provide the full day traces but we can extract the top routes.

[10:22] Maya: Great. Quick commercial note: when you move to Dedicated the pricing math changes — we can show both committed and pay-as-you-go numbers in the next pack.

[10:31] Olivia: One more question on observability — can we get per-token latency breakdowns and tracing to see which kernel call is taking time?
[10:38] Liam: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-route and token-level traces for runs we instrument. We'll grant you observer access for the POC so you can drill into the trace.

[10:48] Sarah: Any notes on deployment complexity for Private? We have an on-prem air-gapped requirement for a couple of customers downstream, is that supported?
[10:55] Maya: We have an on-prem package and a Private deployment option — it requires some infra prep but we've done air-gapped installs for regulated customers. We'll pair you with the private deployment team if you want to go that route.

[11:10] Carlos: Ok logistics — what do you need from us this week?
[11:13] Maya: The action items are: we will share the full benchmark CSV and attach raw logs; Liam will run KV cache + 99th tests and share results; you (Carlos/Sarah) to send sample traces and confirm top routes; schedule the 70B run and the sustained 6-hour run.

[11:30] Olivia: Let's also schedule a deep-dive on quantization kernels — some of our infra folks want to understand the tradeoffs. Week of Apr 20 works for us.

[11:38] Maya: Noted. I'll propose 3 slots after the call.

[11:42] Sarah: Quick question — we listed Anthropic and OpenAI in the vendor comparison, can you include a short appendix comparing approximate cost/latency for those too?
[11:49] Liam: We can include high-level competitive numbers but not full apples-to-apples since hardware and model weights differ. We'll call out the caveats.

[11:58] Maya: Anything else?
[12:00] Carlos: No, that's it from me.
[12:03] Olivia: Good. Thanks everyone.
[12:05] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and schedule.

-- End --

Notes about transcript quality: occasional mislabels (Speaker 1/2), small transcription errors like 'KV cash' or 'quantiziation' in the raw automated notes; will attach original recording if needed.
